## Teaching points

1. Fever, back pain and a neurological deficit occur together in only a small minority of spinal epidural abscesses (about 8% in one review); fever is absent in more than half.
2. Back pain with infection red flags (recent bacterial infection, possible bacteremia, injection drug use, unexplained leukocytosis) needs ESR and CRP and a low threshold for MRI; misdiagnosis at the first ED visit is common.
3. Hyperreflexia, clonus, sensory loss and urinary retention indicate cord compression; measure the bladder volume.
4. CT, even with contrast, can miss an epidural abscess; gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the symptomatic spine is the test of choice.
5. Once deficits appear, emergent decompression plus IV antibiotics is the standard, and the neurological status at surgery largely determines recovery.
